guide.summary: Unit 6 introduces formal inference with proportions: confidence intervals and significance tests for one proportion and for the difference between two proportions, interpretation of confidence levels and P-values, sample-size planning, Type I and Type II errors, and power. The four-step process (State, Plan, Do, Conclude) is graded on every inference FRQ.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals for p
sections.body: Interval: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). Conditions: Random (random sample or random assignment), 10% (n ≤ 10% of population when sampling without replacement), Large Counts (np̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10, using successes and failures). Interpretation: 'We are 95% confident that the interval from __ to __ captures the true proportion of [context].' Confidence level: in many random samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the true proportion. Margin of error grows with higher confidence and shrinks with larger n (by a factor of √n). To guarantee ME ≤ m, solve z*·√(p*(1 − p*)/n) ≤ m, using p* = 0.5 if no estimate is available, and round n up.

sections.heading: Significance tests for p
sections.body: H₀: p = p₀; Hₐ: p <, >, or ≠ p₀ (in terms of the parameter, defined in context). Test statistic: z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); note the SE uses p₀, and Large Counts uses np₀ and n(1 − p₀). The P-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of getting a sample statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the observed one, in the direction of Hₐ. Compare to α: if P ≤ α, reject H₀ and there is convincing evidence for Hₐ; if P > α, fail to reject H₀ and there is not convincing evidence for Hₐ. Never 'accept' H₀. A two-sided test at α corresponds to a (1 − α) confidence interval: if p₀ is outside the interval, reject.

sections.heading: Errors and power
sections.body: Type I error: rejecting H₀ when it is true (P = α). Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when Hₐ is true (P = β). Power = 1 − β = probability of correctly rejecting a false H₀. Power increases with a larger sample size, a larger α, and a true parameter farther from p₀. Describe the consequences of each error in context; choose a smaller α when a Type I error is more serious.

sections.heading: Two proportions
sections.body: Interval: (p̂₁ − p̂₂) ± z*·√(p̂₁(1 − p̂₁)/n₁ + p̂₂(1 − p̂₂)/n₂). Test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0 uses the pooled proportion p̂_c = (x₁ + x₂)/(n₁ + n₂) in the SE: √(p̂_c(1 − p̂_c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)). Conditions apply to both samples (independent random samples or random assignment; Large Counts for all four counts). If an interval for p₁ − p₂ contains 0, there is no convincing evidence of a difference; if entirely positive, convincing evidence that p₁ > p₂.

sections.heading: Worked example: a confidence interval
sections.body: In a random sample of 500 adults, 285 say they exercise regularly, so p̂ = 0.57. A 95% confidence interval is 0.57 ± 1.96√(0.57 × 0.43/500) = 0.57 ± 0.043, or (0.527, 0.613). Interpretation: we are 95% confident that the interval from 52.7% to 61.3% captures the true proportion of all adults who exercise regularly. The confidence level means that about 95% of intervals constructed this way from repeated samples would capture the true proportion.

sections.heading: Worked example: a significance test
sections.body: A company claims 80% of customers are satisfied. In a random sample of 150 customers, 111 are satisfied (p̂ = 0.74). Test H₀: p = 0.80 versus Hₐ: p < 0.80. The test statistic is z = (0.74 − 0.80)/√(0.80 × 0.20/150) ≈ −1.84, and the P-value is about 0.033. At α = 0.05, reject H₀: there is convincing evidence that fewer than 80% of customers are satisfied. Use p₀, not p̂, in the standard deviation for tests.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students interpret confidence levels as probabilities that the parameter is in a specific interval, forget to state conclusions in context, and accept the null hypothesis instead of failing to reject it.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know confidence interval, margin of error, confidence level, null and alternative hypotheses, test statistic, P-value, significance level, Type I and II errors, and power.

keyTakeaways: CI: p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n); test SE uses p₀.
P-value: probability of a result this extreme assuming H₀ is true.
Reject if P ≤ α; never accept H₀.
Type I: reject true H₀; Type II: miss a false H₀.
Power ↑ with larger n, larger α, larger effect.
Two-prop test uses the pooled p̂.
commonMistakes: Saying '95% chance the true proportion is in this interval.'
Using p̂ instead of p₀ in the test's SE and Large Counts check.
Concluding without context or without linking to α.
examTips: Name the procedure exactly (e.g., 'one-sample z-test for a proportion').
Conclusions must include: decision, comparison to α, and context about Hₐ.
Error questions: describe the error in context, then its consequence.
guide.cramSheet:
**CI:** p̂ ± z*√(p̂q̂/n) · 90%: 1.645 · 95%: 1.96 · 99%: 2.576

**Conditions:** Random · 10% · Large Counts (≥ 10)

**Sample size:** n ≥ (z*/m)²p*(1 − p*) · p* = 0.5 · round up

**Test:** z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀q₀/n) · P ≤ α → reject

**Errors:** I = reject true H₀ (α) · II = fail to reject false H₀ (β) · power = 1 − β

**Two-prop:** CI unpooled · test pooled p̂_c

vocab.definition: An interval of plausible values for a parameter, computed as statistic ± margin of error.
The long-run capture rate of the interval-construction method in repeated sampling.
The maximum expected difference between the statistic and the parameter at a given confidence level.
The claim of no effect or no difference, tested against the alternative.
The claim the study seeks evidence for.
Probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a statistic as extreme as or more extreme than observed.
The threshold for rejecting H₀; the probability of a Type I error.
Rejecting H₀ when it is actually true.
Failing to reject H₀ when the alternative is true.
Probability of rejecting H₀ when a particular alternative is true.
Combined proportion of successes in two samples, used in the two-proportion test.
An estimate of the standard deviation of a statistic's sampling distribution.

practice.topic: 6.3 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of a city's residents who recycle is (0.57, 0.67). Which interpretation is correct?

choices.text: 95% of residents recycle between 57% and 67% of the time.
95% of samples will have a sample proportion between 0.57 and 0.67.
There is a 95% probability that the sample proportion is between 0.57 and 0.67.
We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.57 to 0.67 captures the true proportion of residents who recycle.

practice.explanation: The interval estimates the population parameter, with confidence attached to the method.

distractors.C: The sample proportion is known (0.62); it's the center.

practice.topic: 6.4 Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: A company claims 90% of its customers are satisfied. A consumer group suspects the true proportion is lower. Which hypotheses are appropriate?
practice.explanation: Hypotheses use the parameter p; the alternative matches the suspicion (lower).

practice.stem: A test of H₀: the new drug is no more effective than the old drug, versus Hₐ: the new drug is more effective. A Type I error would be

choices.text: concluding the new drug is not more effective when it actually is
concluding the new drug is more effective when it actually is not
correctly concluding the new drug is more effective
using too small a sample

practice.explanation: Type I: rejecting a true null.

practice.topic: 6.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: Holding everything else constant, which change makes a confidence interval for p narrower?

choices.text: Increasing the confidence level from 95% to 99%
Decreasing the sample size
Increasing the sample size
Using a nonrandom sample

practice.explanation: Larger n reduces the standard error.

practice.topic: 6.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: In a random sample of 400 adults, 248 (62%) support a policy. What is the 95% confidence interval for the population proportion?

distractors.B: Uses SE as the margin of error.

practice.topic: 6.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: A pollster wants a 95% confidence interval for a proportion with margin of error at most 0.03 and has no prior estimate. What is the minimum sample size?

distractors.C: Rounds down, which gives ME slightly above 0.03.

practice.topic: 6.6 Concluding a Test for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.50 vs. Hₐ: p > 0.50 yields a P-value of 0.012. Which interpretation of the P-value is correct?

choices.text: There is a 1.2% probability that H₀ is true.
1.2% of the sample supports H₀.
There is a 98.8% probability that Hₐ is true.
Assuming p = 0.50, there is a 1.2% probability of getting a sample proportion as large as or larger than the one observed, by chance alone.

practice.explanation: The P-value is computed assuming H₀; it's about the data, not the hypothesis.

practice.stem: Which change would increase the power of a significance test, all else equal?

choices.text: Decreasing α from 0.05 to 0.01
Increasing the sample size
Testing an alternative closer to the null value
Using a two-sided test instead of a one-sided test in the correct direction

practice.explanation: Larger n reduces the SE, making true differences easier to detect.

practice.topic: 6.11 Carrying Out a Test for the Difference of Two Population Proportions
practice.stem: In a randomized experiment, 45 of 150 patients on a new treatment improved, compared with 30 of 150 on a standard treatment. What is the test statistic for H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0?

practice.topic: 6.9 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Difference Between Population Proportions
practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for p_men − p_women, the difference in proportions who prefer a product, is (−0.04, 0.09). Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: Men are more likely than women to prefer the product.
Men and women definitely have equal preferences.
There is no convincing evidence of a difference, because 0 is in the interval.
Women are more likely to prefer the product.

practice.explanation: Zero is a plausible value for the difference.

distractors.B: Failing to find a difference isn't proof of equality.

practice.topic: 6.5 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: In a random sample of 200 voters, 116 support a candidate. For H₀: p = 0.50 vs. Hₐ: p > 0.50, what are the test statistic and P-value?
A city tests H₀: the lead level in its water is at the safe limit vs. Hₐ: it exceeds the safe limit. Which choice of α is most appropriate, and why?

choices.text: α = 0.01, to minimize the chance of falsely declaring the water unsafe
α = 0.10, because a Type II error (failing to detect unsafe water) has serious health consequences, and a larger α increases power
α = 0.05 always
α doesn't affect the probability of either error

practice.explanation: Missing a real danger is the worse error here; raising α reduces β.

practice.topic: 6.3 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
practice.stem: A 99% confidence interval for p is (0.42, 0.51). Which statement must be true about a two-sided test of H₀: p = 0.52?

choices.text: H₀ would be rejected at α = 0.01.
H₀ would not be rejected at α = 0.01.
H₀ would not be rejected at α = 0.05.
The P-value is greater than 0.05.

practice.explanation: 0.52 lies outside the 99% interval, so a two-sided test at α = 0.01 rejects it (and so would α = 0.05).

practice.topic: 6.8 Confidence Intervals for the Difference of Two Proportions
practice.stem: Using the data 45/150 (new) and 30/150 (standard), what is a 95% confidence interval for p_new − p_standard?

distractors.B: Uses pooled SE = 0.05 for an interval.

practice.topic: 6.5 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion
practice.prompt: A delivery company advertises that 80% of its packages arrive on time. A consumer group takes a random sample of 250 of the company's deliveries from the past year (over 500,000 deliveries) and finds that 188 arrived on time. Do the data provide convincing evidence, at α = 0.05, that fewer than 80% of the company's packages arrive on time?

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and P-value.

rubric.description: H₀: p = 0.80; Hₐ: p < 0.80, where p = the true proportion of all the company's packages that arrive on time.
One-sample z-test for a proportion. Random: random sample. 10%: 250 < 10% of 500,000. Large Counts: 250(0.8) = 200 ≥ 10 and 250(0.2) = 50 ≥ 10.
Because P ≈ 0.029 < 0.05, reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of the company's packages that arrive on time is less than 0.80.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) H₀: p = 0.80 and Hₐ: p < 0.80, where p is the true proportion of all of this company's packages that arrive on time.

(b) One-sample z-test for a population proportion.
Random: the deliveries were a random sample.
10%: 250 is less than 10% of the more than 500,000 deliveries.
Large Counts: np₀ = 250(0.80) = 200 and n(1 − p₀) = 250(0.20) = 50 are both at least 10.

(c) p̂ = 188/250 = 0.752. z = (0.752 − 0.80)/√(0.80 × 0.20/250) = −0.048/0.0253 ≈ −1.90. P-value = P(Z ≤ −1.90) ≈ 0.029.

(d) Because the P-value of 0.029 is less than α = 0.05, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of this company's packages that arrive on time is less than 80%.
